subject: baku
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: baku, the dream-eating tapir spirit.
Style: ukiyo-e woodblock print.
reasoning:
I'm thinking through the design of a baku — the Japanese dream-eating chimeric spirit with a bear's body, elephant trunk, and rhino eyes — and how to render it in ukiyo-e woodblock style using the 3js-builder SDK.

For the visual language, I'm drawing on Edo-period conventions: bold sumi outlines, flat colors in indigo, vermilion, ochre, and cream, plus seigaiha wave patterns, kasumi mist bands, karakusa scrollwork, flame motifs, and Japanese cartouche text, all layered with subtle woodgrain texture.

For a 3D version, I'm thinking of cel-shading with flat colors and faux ink outlines placed at silhouette edges, since true view-dependent outlines aren't directly available. I want to compose the baku's body like a karajishi — stocky, lion-bear-like, with a broad head, swirling mane curls in indigo and white, striped legs, and flame motifs at the haunches.

I'm detailing the head: a ridged trunk, curved ivory tusks, rhino-like eyes drawn with bold ukiyo-e ink lines and kabuki-style kumadori red accents, and a spiral-curled mane in indigo with vermilion tips, set against a stocky tan or indigo-toned body typical of traditional baku depictions.

Now I'm weighing body color schemes—thinking a black/indigo front and hindquarters with a white saddle band (echoing the Malayan tapir, the real-world animal baku is based on), patterned with seigaiha or karakusa motifs, while blending in chimera traits like tiger-striped legs and a tufted ox tail.

Combining a vermilion mane, indigo body with white scroll patterns, cream underside, ochre tiger-striped legs, gold-capped ivory tusks, and cloud wisps at the feet feels visually strong, but I need to stick to the brief's instruction that nothing beyond the subject itself should appear—so no scenery, no floating dream-mist props, even though the "dream-eating" concept tempts me to add something extra.

Flame and cloud-wisp motifs on the shoulders and haunches work since they're part of the creature's mythological design, similar to how qilin or komainu carry flame tufts on their legs—so I'll keep those as integral features rather than separate props. I'm settling on a target of roughly 250–300 parts, 8–10 textures, and about 1000 lines, and now I'm working out proportions based on a real tapir's size before scaling up the mythical baku form.

I'm sizing it a bit larger and more stylized than a real tapir—body length around 1.9–2.4 m with the trunk, shoulder height ~1.2 m, mane rising to ~1.45 m—using the +Y up, +Z forward coordinate convention. Now I'm sketching the skeleton: a spine chain from hips through neck to head, a six-joint tail, a five-joint trunk chain off the head, a separate jaw, four three-segment legs with toe/claw details, and small jointed ears.

I'm planning a quadruped build using IK limbs for the legs, giving the front legs a straighter stance with elbows back and the hind legs a forward knee/back hock for a stocky, lion-like posture with big paws. For the torso I'm thinking of a swept/lofted spine chain with variable radius so the belly hangs naturally, and I'm roughing out key coordinates—ground at y=0, paw radius ~0.07 m, hips around (0, 0.95, -0.55), torso spanning roughly z=-0.75 to z=0.55 at spine height ~0.95 m.

Using a sole hint of [0,0,1] would keep the paw flat along the forward axis, like a foot lying flat on the ground, but for digitigrade paws I want the toes angled forward while the metacarpals tilt up, so I'll go with a simpler approximation instead.

Let me settle on naming: leg chains use shoulder/elbow/wrist/hand for front legs and hip/knee/ankle/foot for hind legs, with the paw itself built from a squashed box part plus cone claws and small sphere toes attached at the tip joint. For roles, I'll just tag all four legs as "leg" rather than distinguishing arm vs leg, keeping things simple.

Trunk fits as a tentacle chain, the tail stays "tail", and mane joints could use the "fan" role. For toes, instead of adding full joint chains for each digit, I'll attach toes directly as extra parts off each paw bone to avoid bloating the joint count -- though if digit joints are needed later, each toe could just be a single-joint chain tagged "digit" off the hand/foot joint.

Settling on anatomical accuracy modeled after a tapir: 4 toes on each front paw and 3 on each hind paw, giving 14 toe joints total, built through a shared paw-making helper function.

For the head, I'm thinking of a tapir/baku hybrid skull — elongated with pronounced brow ridges, a drooping proboscis, a short tusked muzzle, and a separately jointed lower jaw so it can open and close independently from the cranium.

The trunk itself should sweep from the muzzle, curving down and forward, then curling up at the tip like a resting elephant trunk, with a small fingerlike nub at the end echoing a tapir's proboscis. I'll add ring ridges along it using torus segments for texture, and I'm now considering how to render the eyes — small and deep-set like a rhino's, but stylized for a ukiyo-e feel.

For the eyes, I'll go bold: gold irises with black pupils, thick black outlines, a vermilion kumadori ring around an almond shape, and a white highlight, with curling indigo eyebrow tufts above like a karajishi's flared brows, using decals on the head surface. For the ears, I'm picturing rounded tapir-like shapes with white or cream tips rather than lion ears.

For the mane, I'm planning stylized spiral curls like karajishi scrollwork — building swirl-shaped cards with black outlines, indigo fill, and white highlight lines, scattering dozens across the neck, shoulders, and chest. I'm also weighing whether extruded 3D swirl shapes would read better than flat cards from a distance.

I'm working out the geometry for a tapered spiral ribbon shape — a logarithmic spiral centerline with decreasing width toward the tip — making sure the curl winds without self-intersecting.

A curl is really just one turn of a comma-like shape, so I can generate the outline procedurally with trig functions and extrude it with no smoothing. With around 40 curls each needing roughly 40 outline points, I'm estimating the triangle count will scale accordingly.

Alternatively, I could sweep a tube along a spiral path for 3D horn-like curls, which would be cheap and low-poly, but a flat extruded swirl ribbon with slight thickness and bevel edges feels closer to the ukiyo-e flat-print look, especially if I paint it with an indigo-to-white gradient along its length. I think the authentic ukiyo-e feel will mostly come from palette choices like indigo tones.

Also, text rendering is risky since Japanese characters might show as tofu boxes without a CJK font available, so instead of real kanji I'm considering drawing a simplified red seal (hanko) with abstract stroke-like paths mimicking a stylized mark rather than an actual character.

Maybe a safer route is a hanko-style emblem instead—a red square seal with a stylized crescent moon or swirling tomoe pattern to evoke dreams and night, rather than risking illegible kanji.

What would really delight is leaning into ukiyo-e print aesthetics: flat saturated colors with bold outlines in a Hokusai/Kuniyoshi style, since those artists' monsters have richly patterned bodies. I'm picturing the Edo-era baku depictions—lion-like with an elephant trunk—as my reference point.

I'm sketching out the body details: curled fur, striped legs, an ox-like tail with a tuft, and claws, with a wide-nostriled trunk and large eyes. For colors, I'm drawn to an "aizuri-e" approach—prints dominated by indigo blues with touches of vermilion and cream for the belly, tusks, and ear rims, giving it that classic blue-print elegance.

For the body design, I'm weighing a Malayan tapir-style two-tone pattern—dark front and hindquarters with a lighter cream or white saddle in the middle—since that black-and-cream contrast against vermilion mane curls feels like a striking ukiyo-e combination. I'm also considering giving the pale saddle a subtle seigaiha wave pattern in light blue, with the indigo sections carrying white scroll arabesques for added texture.

Now I'm settling on a final palette: indigo body, cream saddle, ochre tiger-striped legs, vermilion and indigo mane curls with cream edges, black outlines, and gold accents—a harmonious indigo-orange complementary scheme. I'm also thinking through how to render the body paint to keep that flat, woodblock-print look rather than realistic shading, considering options like toon-style two-tone cel shading versus a fully flat emissive approach.

Rather than relying on an external toon kit that might not resolve reliably, I'm deciding to reimplement a simple cel-shading helper myself using the core SDK's paint, mix, and noise utilities, keeping the glow kit in reserve for things like glowing eyes or flame effects.

Though ukiyo-e style typically skips glow, the prompt notes that lanterns, fire, crystals, and magic can glow — so I'm thinking of giving this dream-eating spirit a flaming hōju jewel on its forehead, echoing the Buddhist cintamani/wish-granting jewel motif often paired with baku and shishi imagery, rendered in glowing gold-vermilion as a spirit identity cue.

I'm leaning toward embedding it like an urna mark rather than floating it above the head, and considering subtle flame-scroll (kaen) accents on the shoulders with a muted glow strength around 0.6 to stay consistent with the flat print aesthetic. I also need to decide whether to import the glow helper from the style kit or reimplement the short emissive-material function locally.

I could implement glow manually, but since the kit explicitly supports this and is "tested," it makes more sense to just import glow from the kit rather than reinventing it.

Actually for ukiyo-e shading I want a bokashi gradient effect rather than standard cel shadows, so I'll write my own flat paint combos instead of relying on the cel kit. I'll just import `glow` from its kit for self-lit surfaces.

But I'm second-guessing whether importing a kit subpath is even safe, since the SDK docs say every export comes from one module and if the app's import map only maps "three" and "agentic-3js-builder" without the kit subpaths, importing "agentic-3js-builder/kits/glow" directly could fail at load time and break everything. Given that risk, writing my own small glow implementation for the few parts that need it seems like the safer bet.

I'm also weighing whether to use three/addons' BufferGeometryUtils for merging geometries, but since part counts stay well under 1000, skipping merging is fine and avoids an unnecessary import risk. For performance, since the paint sheet bakes each painted part once, running a 3-octave Perlin noise paint over roughly 20-30 parts at 1024 paint size should still be comfortably fast. For the ukiyo-e look, I'm thinking about faking key-block outlines by duplicating and slightly scaling up geometry for major body parts as an inverted hull, since the engine doesn't render outlines natively.

I'm working out how to simulate a back-face outline shell without being able to set material side directly, since SDK parts share a front-face-only MeshStandardMaterial per color — flipping the triangle winding of an enlarged duplicate mesh so its normals face inward would let the camera see the far inner surface as a silhouette outline, effectively faking a backside-render outline using only front-face materials.

The trickier part is getting a uniform offset shell: for primitives I construct myself I can offset vertices along their normals, but for swept/lofted geometry from the SDK I'd need to read the generated mesh data and duplicate it with flipped winding and normal displacement, which gets complicated further for skinned meshes where I'd also need to carry over skin indices, weights, and bone data to keep the shell following deformations correctly.

For sphere-based parts I could keep smooth normals, displace the shell outward, then flip winding and normals so it reads as ink from inside-out. For tubes though, a bigger duplicate sweep would just occlude the inner one rather than ring it, so the outline trick doesn't translate as cleanly there.

I'm thinking I can flip the winding post-hoc by swapping index pairs per triangle and negating normals — since tubes get re-deformed from skin weights on the CPU after posing, this geometry edit shouldn't interfere with that process, and since I won't be querying surface normals on these outline meshes, flipping them is safe. The exporter merges everything into one geometry afterward, so winding order is preserved through to final output.

My plan is an `outline(sweep, thickness)` helper that rebuilds a sweep with added radius, flips its winding, and colors it as ink, applying the same approach to tubes and lofted bodies. This roughly doubles triangle count for those parts but stays within budget, though I need to watch for cases where the flipped shell's inner faces become visible at silhouette edges if the outer mesh doesn't fully occlude them.

Thinking about outline thickness: with a constant δ, the silhouette width scales with world units, so for a 1.9m body I'd want δ around 1-1.5% of length (about 2cm) for bold woodblock-style lines, scaling down to 6-8mm for smaller parts like toes and tusks.

I'm checking whether flipping winding order is legitimate within the builder's conventions — since everything joins through `b.part`/sweep helpers, flipping index order post-creation should be fine, but I need to consider how the export harness handles negative-winding meshes, since it merges parts into one mesh with default FrontSide material. If I flip winding without flipping normals, the lighting on inverted-hull surfaces would compute using outward-facing normals on what's now an inner wall — though for near-black ink coloring this error might not visibly matter.

Now I'm working out the ground-contact rule: the model's lowest points should touch or sink slightly below the floor, up to 2% of total height (roughly 2.9cm for a 1.45m model). I want to keep the paw outline offset small, aiming for the lowest point including outlines to sit around -0.006 rather than sinking too deep.

I'm weighing whether the inverted-hull outline technique is worth the risk for the ukiyo-e aesthetic — it should give a strong linework effect, but I'm wary of correctness issues on smooth-skinned sweep geometry.

For sweeps, the outline shell is just a wider-radius sweep with flipped winding; for primitive shapes like spheres and ellipsoids, I can scale each axis slightly outward to get a roughly constant-thickness shell, then flip the winding order to make it render inside-out as an outline. I'm writing a helper that reverses triangle winding on indexed geometry so these outline shells face correctly.

I'm also checking that flat outline colors bypass the paint-bake UV charts entirely, so the flipped winding won't interfere with how paint gets rasterized — since outlines use a solid flat color rather than a texture chart, this should be safe.

Shells sharing the same bone chain as the main mesh should inherit identical skin weights automatically, which is good for consistent deformation. I'm also thinking through potential z-fighting: since shells are offset outward by a small delta, they shouldn't be coplanar with the main surface, though overlapping body parts (like a leg shell poking into the torso) could still cause hidden geometry issues that get masked by the outer body surface.

From the side, the leg is a vertical cylinder and the shell's inward-facing wall becomes visible just beyond the leg's silhouette edges, creating a dark outline band on either side that continues upward to meet the torso surface.

Now I'm planning the SVG textures and paints — like a glaring ukiyo-e eye decal with red kumadori and golden iris, plus other decorative card elements to layer on.

I'm sketching more textures: a vermilion-and-gold flame tuft for the haunches and tail, a seigaiha wave pattern computed as a custom paint on the saddle surface, and a karakusa scroll decal for additional ornamentation.

Thinking further, I want spiral/tomoe joint-swirl decals in cream and vermilion placed at the shoulders and hips, echoing the traditional "joint spiral" markings seen on karajishi figures to strengthen the mythical-lion feel. Beyond that I'm planning a forehead hanko seal mark, tufted tail cards, and curled mane-lock cards.

Now I'm considering cloud-wisp (kasumi) ornaments clinging to the ankles like flame-wreaths on a komainu or qilin—these count as creature features rather than extra scenery, so they fit the brief's constraint, and I want big bulging ringed eyes like those in baku woodblock prints, plus an overall silhouette with a heavy-browed, oversized head to push the stylization further.

Working out the body design: a lion-tapir quadruped in a resting stance with its trunk coiling forward then curling up, closed jaw built as separate upper/lower parts so it can open, a tufted ox tail curled at the tip, and four legs spread with flat paws. I'm sketching the skeleton's spine coordinates from hips to neck to establish the pose.

I'm reconsidering the torso proportions, leaning toward a lion-bear-sized baku with shoulder height around 1.1m, arching the back gently rather than making it too tall, and calculating the belly line and leg length so the proportions feel balanced between tapir and mythical beast.

Now I'm plotting out the spine as a series of control points from tail root through hips, mid-back, chest, neck base, and up to the skull, keeping the neck thick and short so the head sits lower relative to the shoulders, true to a tapir's build.

I'm thinking through the skeleton hierarchy next: hips as the root joint, with hind legs branching off the hips and front legs off the chest joint, then building a spine chain from hips forward through named segments up to the neck.

For the spine/neck chain, I'm mapping six points to joints named spine1-3 and neck1-2, then adding a separate head joint as a child of the last neck joint so I can control its forward-and-down aim independently of the chain's natural tangent.

For the tail and torso, I'm thinking I need the rump to sit behind the hips joint, so the body sweep can extend past the root. The cleanest fix is probably repositioning the hips joint itself slightly forward of the rump point, letting the torso and tail sweeps share that root properly.

I could put the root "hips" joint at the pelvis location with hind leg hip joints as children offset slightly, which is how many rigs handle pelvis placement. Or alternatively, I could have the body path start right at the hips joint with a round cap, since a round cap naturally extends beyond the path's start point.

The rump extends back roughly a radius-width past the hips position, forming a dome shape, and that's where the tail root attaches. For the torso, I'm considering using a loft rather than a simple sweep, since a loft lets width and height vary independently per station -- useful for giving the lion's chest a broader-than-tall silhouette.

Setting station widths/heights across roughly seven points from rump to chest, I'm also thinking about whether the neck should get its own sweep (thick, tapering toward the skull) separate from the mane curls wrapped around it, or whether to unify spine and neck into one continuous loft for a seamless mesh, with the head modeled separately afterward.

Before writing the actual builder code, I want to double-check the SDK's exact call signatures — createBuilder, joint, chain, and sweep — so I use parameters like bone, caps, sides, and twist correctly without guessing at unclear semantics.

I'm also reviewing loft (for building the torso via station profiles), part, stick, surface, and decal, so I have the full toolkit mapped out before committing to the implementation.

Continuing through the API surface, I'm noting extrude, lathe, cards, ring, along, and various primitive shapers like spike, rod, capsule, and frustumBox, plus sprout for generating child elements along a structure.

I'm also cataloging pose and limb for skeletal positioning, the full paint toolkit (mix, noise, cells, stripes, scales, gradient, grain, etc.) for surfacing, frame and line helpers for spatial reference, basic math utilities like aim, lerp, and vec, and path generators like arc, bezier, and spiral.

Now I'm planning the color palette, keeping flat colors limited since they count against the 64-color budget, while paints don't — settling on a sumi ink, washi cream, indigo body tones, and vermilion accents for a traditional palette.

For the print style I'm considering adding subtle noise-based grain to mimic ukiyo-e bokashi gradients and woodgrain texture in the paints.

I want to define a helper for print-style paints using toon-like cel shading, where the light-to-shade threshold creates that flat woodblock print look.

Actually, hard two-tone shading reads as "toon" rather than true ukiyo-e, since woodblock prints are flat colour with just line work. A better approach combines flat base colour with a soft bokashi-style gradient (lighter at top, darker at belly) plus wood grain texture, letting the scene's natural lighting add subtle shading without baking in too much.

Now I'm working out the seigaiha wave pattern for the saddle — overlapping concentric arcs built from lattice-positioned circles with offset rows, choosing coordinate planes based on whether the surface faces sideways or upward. Writing pattern math...

I'm trying to work out the overlap direction for the arcs—whether upper rows cover lower rows or vice versa, like comparing roof tiles to how fish-scale (uroko) versus wave (seigaiha) motifs stack their curves.

With row spacing of R/2 and alternating horizontal offsets, each circle's visible top portion gets covered by the row below it, so I need to figure out, for a given point, which row's circle actually renders there on top.

Working out detection logic...

Only about 4 rows fall within range, so the overlap check stays cheap, and I can map distance ratios into rings with alternating washi and pale ink tones for a layered texture effect.

I'm estimating the total painted surface area to gauge pixel density: torso, legs, head, neck, and tail together come to roughly 6 m², with mane curls potentially adding more if they're painted rather than flat-colored.

Now I'm planning the actual paint textures needed: a body indigo paint with subtle woodgrain and mottling, lighter near the top and darkening toward the belly, following a Malayan tapir-style color split with darker forequarters and hindquarters and a lighter saddle in between.

For the saddle region, I'm considering a cream band with pale-blue seigaiha wave patterns, bordered by a wavy "kasumi"-style cloud edge rendered with ink outlines and a thin vermilion accent line, echoing ukiyo-e garment cartouche motifs rather than a plain straight boundary.

I'm defining the saddle's vertical extent and wavy edges in model space, letting the band wrap fully around the circumference with a sinusoidal boundary so it reads as a stylized tapir marking, while the belly beneath fades back to cream. Next I'm planning the legs in ochre with black tiger-stripe bands running around each limb.

I'll also add curl tufts at the back of elbows and hocks, plus flame-wreaths at the ankles. For the head, I'm thinking indigo-black with the trunk sides in a similar dark tone, keeping it consistent with a real tapir's coloring rather than contrasting with a cream muzzle.

Now I'm mapping the full color palette to establish focal hierarchy: the face as centerpiece with gold eyes rimmed in red, ivory tusks, a deep indigo trunk with lighter blue ring lines, a cream muzzle with whisker spots, a forehead gem, and vermilion brow tufts. For the mane, I'm working out alternating vermilion and indigo curls circling the head and neck, drawing on how karajishi art typically renders mane colors.

I'm thinking through how to shade the extruded curl geometry using surface normals to distinguish wall faces from front faces, applying ink coloring to the walls and gradient coloring to the front faces, though I'm wrestling with how to detect proximity to the outline edge for a cleaner ink border.

Actually, a better approach might be drawing each curl as an SVG with its own ink outline and inner swirl details, then applying that as a textured card — cheap flat quads that give a strong hand-drawn look, with rings of these cards arranged around the neck at varying depths and orientations so the mane reads with volume from any viewing angle.

Maybe simpler: extruded flat curl shapes radiating outward like petals around the neck, each lying in a plane that contains the radial and circumferential directions — similar to how a karajishi lion's mane curls are depicted.

This is the most readable approach: scale-armor arrangement where curls lie across the surface like overlapping spiral shingles, so from any viewpoint the neck appears covered in spiral curls. I'll place curl geometry along the stick shapes to build this effect.

Working out orientation frame for extrusion...

I'll go with thickness around 0.03 and a slight lift so pieces overlap like shingles, adding a small random tilt around b so each scale sticks up for a layered 3D look.

For the mane covering neck, chest, and shoulders, I'm estimating 60-90 curls, each contributing roughly 100-160 triangles, totaling around 12k triangles which fits the 60k budget. Each curl counts as its own part, so that's about 90 parts toward my target of 180-340, and I'm now budgeting parts for the torso with a loft and outline.

Totaling it all up, I'm landing around 250-300 pieces, with the neck folded into the mane's loft rather than separate parts.
